topics.title: What is science?
topics.html:
Science is the systematic study of the natural and physical world through observation and experiment, to explain how things work.

BranchStudies
Biologyliving things
Chemistrysubstances and how they change
Physicsenergy, forces and matter

Science vs technology: science finds out why and how things happen. Technology applies scientific knowledge to make useful products and solve problems (e.g. science of electricity → phones, MRT).

topics.title: What is the nature of scientific knowledge?
topics.html:
• Based on evidence: ideas must be supported by observations and data that others can check
  • Tentative: it can change when new evidence appears (e.g. the Earth-centred model of the universe was replaced by the Sun-centred model. Models of the atom changed many times)
  • Tested and shared: scientists repeat experiments and review each other's work before accepting results
  • A theory explains why something happens. A law describes what always happens
Watch out: "tentative" doesn't mean science is a guess. It means scientists change their ideas when better evidence appears.

topics.title: How do we practise science?
topics.html:
Observe → Ask a question → Hypothesis → Plan a fair test → Collect data → Analyse → Conclude → Communicate

VariableMeaningExample: does temperature affect how fast sugar dissolves?
Independentwhat you changewater temperature
Dependentwhat you measuretime for sugar to dissolve
Controlled (constant)what you keep the same for a fair testmass of sugar, volume of water, stirring

Good practice: repeat readings and take an average, read measuring cylinders at eye level at the bottom of the meniscus, use SI units (m, kg, s, °C).

Hazard symbolMeaning
Flameflammable: catches fire easily
Skull and crossbonestoxic: poisonous
Liquid eating a hand and metalcorrosive: destroys skin and materials
Exclamation markharmful or irritant
Exploding bombexplosive

Bunsen burner: air hole closed gives a yellow (luminous), sooty, cooler flame. Air hole open gives a blue (non-luminous), hotter flame used for heating.

Watch out: change only one variable at a time, or you can't tell which change caused the result.

topics.title: What influences the way we practise science?
topics.html:
• Values and attitudes: integrity (report results honestly), objectivity (no bias), open-mindedness, curiosity, perseverance
  • Ethics: is it right? e.g. testing on animals, using human data, genetic modification
  • Society and culture: what people need or accept affects what is researched
  • Funding and resources: governments and companies decide what research to pay for
  • Technology: new instruments (microscopes, telescopes, computers) open up new discoveries
  • Safety and environment: research must not harm people or nature

topics.title: Why do we learn science?
topics.html:
• To understand the world around us and how our bodies work
  • To make informed decisions (e.g. health, food, energy use, reading product labels)
  • To solve problems in society (e.g. NEWater, vaccines, clean energy, climate change)
  • To build skills: observing, questioning, reasoning, working with evidence
  • For future careers in science, engineering, medicine and technology

topics.title: Why is it important to know the physical properties of matter?
topics.html:
Matter is anything that has mass and takes up space. Physical properties can be observed or measured without changing what the substance is.

Knowing them lets us choose the right material for a job:

ObjectMaterialProperty used
Cooking potaluminium or steelgood conductor of heat, high melting point
Pot handleplastic or woodpoor conductor of heat
Electrical wirecopper, covered in plasticcopper conducts electricity, plastic insulates
Windowglasstransparent, hard, waterproof
Raincoatplastic or nylonwaterproof, flexible
Watch out: when asked why a material is used, name the property and link it to the job ("copper is used because it is a good conductor of electricity, so current flows easily").

topics.title: What are some common physical properties of matter?
topics.html:
PropertyMeaning
Hardnessresists scratching (diamond is the hardest natural material)
Strengthcan take a large force without breaking
Flexibilitybends without breaking
Elasticityreturns to its original shape after stretching
Malleabilitycan be hammered into thin sheets
Ductilitycan be drawn into wires
Conductivitylets heat or electricity pass through
Melting and boiling pointtemperature at which a solid melts, or a liquid boils
Transparencytransparent (see through clearly), translucent (some light), opaque (no light)
Solubilityhow well it dissolves in a liquid
Densitymass per unit volume (see 2.3)
Magnetismattracted by a magnet (iron, steel, nickel, cobalt)
MetalsNon-metals
shiny, good conductors of heat and electricity, malleable and ductile, usually high melting point, sonorous (ring when hit)dull, poor conductors (except graphite), brittle when solid, usually low melting point
Watch out: mercury is a metal that is liquid at room temperature, and graphite is a non-metal that conducts electricity. These are common MCQ traps.

topics.title: How do we investigate the density of objects?
topics.html:
Density = massvolume   ρ = mV   units: g/cm³ or kg/m³
ObjectHow to find volume
Regular solid (cuboid)measure with a ruler: length × breadth × height
Irregular soliddisplacement: lower it into a measuring cylinder of water. Volume = final reading − initial reading. Or use a displacement can and collect the overflow
Liquidmeasuring cylinder, read at the bottom of the meniscus

Mass is measured with an electronic balance. 1 cm³ = 1 ml. Density of water = 1 g/cm³.

ExampleA stone has a mass of 60 g. Water rises from 50 cm³ to 70 cm³. Volume = 20 cm³. Density = 60 ÷ 20 = 3 g/cm³.
ExampleA block 2 cm × 3 cm × 5 cm has a mass of 240 g. Volume = 30 cm³. Density = 240 ÷ 30 = 8 g/cm³.
Watch out: density doesn't change with size. Cutting a block in half halves the mass and volume, so density stays the same.

topics.title: What are the effects of different densities?
topics.html:
• An object floats if it is less dense than the liquid. It sinks if it is denser
  • Liquids that don't mix form layers: the densest at the bottom (e.g. oil floats on water)
  • Ice (0.92 g/cm³) floats on water (1 g/cm³)
  • A steel ship floats because its hull holds a lot of air, so the average density of the whole ship is less than water
  • A hot-air balloon rises because hot air is less dense than the cooler air around it
  • Objects float more easily in seawater because salt water is denser than fresh water
ExampleWood (0.6 g/cm³) floats in water. Iron (7.9 g/cm³) sinks in water, but floats in mercury (13.6 g/cm³).
Watch out: heavy objects don't always sink. Compare densities, not masses.

topics.title: How can understanding physical properties affect our choices for sustainable living?
topics.html:
Choose materials that do the job and harm the environment less.

ChoiceWhy it is more sustainable
Reusable bottles and bags (durable, strong)used many times, so less waste
Aluminium cans, glass bottlescan be recycled many times
Biodegradable packaging (paper, plant-based)broken down by decomposers
Good insulation in buildingsless energy needed for cooling
Lightweight (low density) materials in vehiclesless fuel needed

Most plastics are durable and cheap but non-biodegradable, so they stay in landfills and oceans for hundreds of years. Singapore's only landfill, Semakau, is expected to fill up, so reducing waste matters.

Reduce → Reuse → Recycle (the 3Rs)

topics.title: Elements, compounds and mixtures compared
topics.html:
ElementCompoundMixture
Definitiona pure substance that cannot be broken down into simpler substances by chemical meansa pure substance of two or more elements chemically combined in a fixed ratiotwo or more substances (elements and/or compounds) not chemically combined
Particle diagram
atoms (e.g. Fe) or molecules of the same atoms (e.g. O₂)
each molecule has atoms of different elements joined (e.g. CO)
different particles mixed, not joined
Types of particleonly one kind of atomone kind of molecule (or fixed ratio of ions)two or more kinds of particle
Pure substance?yesyesno
Compositionfixed (one element)fixed ratio by mass, shown by a formula (water is always H₂O)any proportion (more or less sugar in tea)
Propertiesits own characteristic propertiesdifferent from the elements it is made of (sodium + chlorine → table salt)each part keeps its own properties (iron in iron + sulfur is still magnetic)
Energy change when formednot applicableusually heat or light given out or taken in (a chemical reaction)little or none (just mixing)
Separated or broken down bycannot be broken down chemicallychemical methods only (e.g. electrolysis of water, heating to decompose)physical methods: filtration, evaporation, distillation, chromatography, magnet
Melting and boiling pointsfixed, sharpfixed, sharpmelts or boils over a range of temperatures
Represented bya symbol: Fe, O, Na (or O₂ for oxygen gas)a chemical formula: H₂O, CO₂, NaClno single formula: list the parts (e.g. "sand and water")
Examplesiron, copper, oxygen, hydrogen, carbon, sulfurwater, carbon dioxide, sodium chloride, glucose, calcium carbonateair, seawater, soil, steel (alloy), milk, crude oil, orange juice
Watch out: a compound is not a mixture of elements. In a compound the elements are chemically joined and have new properties. In a mixture nothing is joined and each part keeps its properties.

topics.title: How is understanding chemical composition applicable to our daily lives?
topics.html:
Chemical composition is what a substance is made of. Knowing it helps us:

  • use substances safely (e.g. never mix bleach with other cleaners, as harmful gases can form)
  • read food labels and choose healthier food (sugar, salt, fat content)
  • understand medicines and their doses
  • choose materials for products (e.g. alloys for coins, stainless steel for cutlery)
  • detect harmful substances (e.g. carbon monoxide from burning fuel in a closed room)

topics.title: What are the basic building blocks of matter and their chemically combined derivatives?
topics.html:
• An element is a pure substance that cannot be broken down into simpler substances by chemical means. It is made of only one type of atom
  • There are 118 known elements, arranged in the Periodic Table
  • Elements combine chemically to form compounds (their "chemically combined derivatives")
ElementSymbolElementSymbol
HydrogenHSodiumNa
CarbonCMagnesiumMg
NitrogenNChlorineCl
OxygenOIronFe
HeliumHeCopperCu
SulfurSCalciumCa

Symbols: first letter capital, second letter small (Co = cobalt, but CO = carbon monoxide, a compound).

Elements are grouped as metals (left and centre of the Periodic Table), non-metals (right) and metalloids (in between, e.g. silicon).

topics.title: What matter comprises elements and/or compounds that are not chemically combined?
topics.html:
CompoundMixture
Made oftwo or more elements chemically combinedtwo or more substances not chemically combined
Proportionsfixed (water is always H₂O)can vary (more or less sugar in tea)
Propertiesdifferent from its elementseach part keeps its own properties
Separated bychemical reactions onlyphysical methods (filtering, distillation)
Energy change when formedusually yes (heat or light)usually little or none
Exampleswater, carbon dioxide, sodium chloride (table salt)air, seawater, alloys, soil, orange juice
ExampleSodium (a reactive metal) and chlorine (a poisonous gas) combine to form sodium chloride, which is safe to eat. A compound's properties differ from its elements.
Iron + sulfurMixed: a magnet still pulls out the iron. Heated: they react to form iron sulfide, a new compound that is not magnetic.

Types of mixture: solution (solute dissolved in a solvent, e.g. salt water, clear), suspension (insoluble particles spread in a liquid, e.g. muddy water, settles on standing), alloy (metal mixed with other elements, e.g. steel, brass).

Watch out: air is a mixture, not a compound. Its gases are not chemically combined and the proportions vary.

topics.title: How can we distinguish between elements, compounds and mixtures?
topics.html:
See the full comparison table at the top of this chapter: Elements, compounds and mixtures compared.

  • Purity test: a pure substance melts and boils at a fixed temperature (pure water boils at 100 °C). Impurities lower the melting point and raise the boiling point, and make them happen over a range
  • Chromatography: a pure substance gives one spot. A mixture of dyes gives several spots
Watch out: in particle diagrams, joined circles of the same colour are an element (e.g. O₂). Joined circles of different colours are a compound. Unjoined different particles are a mixture.

topics.title: What is the purpose of separation techniques?
topics.html:
• Obtain useful substances: salt from seawater, sugar from sugar cane, metals from ores
  • Remove impurities or harmful substances: clean drinking water, pure medicines
  • Identify what is in a mixture: testing food colourings, forensic analysis of inks
  • Recycle and reduce waste: separating metals and plastics in recycling plants

topics.title: How do we choose the appropriate separation technique(s)?
topics.html:
Pick the technique based on the property that differs between the parts of the mixture.

MixtureTechniqueProperty used
Magnetic and non-magnetic solids (iron + sand)magnetic attractionmagnetism
Solids of different sizes (rice + sand)sievingparticle size
Insoluble solid + liquid (sand + water)filtration: solid left on the filter paper is the residue, liquid passing through is the filtratesolubility, particle size
Soluble solid from a solution (salt from salt water)evaporation to drynessboiling point
Soluble solid that breaks down on strong heating (sugar, copper(II) sulfate)crystallisation: heat to a saturated solution, then cool so crystals formsolubility falls on cooling
Pure liquid from a solution (water from seawater)simple distillation: boil, then condense the vapour. The liquid collected is the distillateboiling point
Liquids that mix, with different boiling points (ethanol + water)fractional distillationboiling point
Liquids that don't mix (oil + water)separating funneldensity, immiscibility
Dyes in ink or food colouringpaper chromatographysolubility in the solvent

Chromatography tips: draw the start line in pencil (ink would run), keep it above the solvent level, and put a lid on to stop evaporation.

Distillation tips: thermometer bulb at the side arm, cold water enters the condenser at the bottom, add boiling chips for smooth boiling.

Watch out: evaporation gives you the solid and loses the water. Distillation gives you the water (and leaves the solid behind).

topics.title: How can we apply separation techniques to obtain potable water in Singapore?
topics.html:
Potable water is water that is safe to drink. Singapore gets it from the Four National Taps:

TapHow it works
Local catchmentrainwater collected in reservoirs and drains, then treated
Imported waterwater piped from Johor, Malaysia
NEWaterused water treated by microfiltration, reverse osmosis and ultraviolet (UV) disinfection
Desalinationseawater turned into fresh water, mainly by reverse osmosis

Conventional water treatment:

Screening → Coagulation (chemicals clump small particles) → Sedimentation (clumps settle) → Filtration (sand filters) → Chlorination (kills germs) → Storage

  • Microfiltration: removes bacteria and fine particles
  • Reverse osmosis: pressure pushes water through a partially permeable membrane, leaving salts, viruses and other dissolved substances behind
  • UV disinfection: kills any remaining microorganisms
Watch out: name each step and what it removes. Desalination and reverse osmosis use a lot of energy, so they are costly.

topics.title: How do we represent light?
topics.html:
• Light travels in straight lines. We draw it as a ray: a straight line with an arrow showing direction. A beam is many rays
  • Luminous objects give out their own light (Sun, lamp, fire). Non-luminous objects are seen because they reflect light into our eyes (Moon, book)
  • Shadows form when an opaque object blocks light, because light cannot bend around it
MaterialLightExample
Transparentpasses through almost completely, clear imageclear glass, water
Translucentsome passes through, blurred imagefrosted glass, tracing paper
Opaquenone passes throughwood, metal
Watch out: we see objects because light enters our eyes. Arrows go from the object to the eye, never from the eye.

topics.title: What is reflection and what are its applications?
topics.html:
Reflection is the bouncing of light off a surface.

Law of reflection: angle of incidence = angle of reflection   (i = r)
  • Both angles are measured from the normal: a line at 90° to the surface
  • The incident ray, reflected ray and normal all lie in the same plane

Image in a plane mirror: same size as the object, upright, laterally inverted (left and right swapped), as far behind the mirror as the object is in front, and virtual (can't be caught on a screen).

ApplicationHow it uses reflection
Periscopetwo plane mirrors at 45° let you see over obstacles
Rear-view and side mirrorslet drivers see behind them
Convex mirrors at road bends and in shopsgive a wider field of view
"AMBULANCE" written backwardsreads correctly in a driver's mirror (lateral inversion)
ExampleA ray hits a mirror at 30° to the surface. Angle of incidence = 90° − 30° = 60°, so angle of reflection = 60°.
Watch out: always measure angles from the normal, not from the mirror surface.

topics.title: What happens when the reflecting surface is rough?
topics.html:
Regular reflectionDiffuse (irregular) reflection
Surfacesmooth (mirror, still water)rough (paper, wall, clothing)
Reflected raysparallel rays stay parallelscattered in many directions
Imageclear image formedno clear image
  • The law of reflection is still obeyed at every point. The normals point in different directions because the surface is uneven, so the rays scatter
  • Diffuse reflection lets us see objects from any angle, and makes paper easy to read without glare
Watch out: diffuse reflection does not break the law of reflection.

topics.title: What happens when light passes through different mediums?
topics.html:
Marked optional for G2 Science in the textbook.

Refraction is the bending of light when it passes from one transparent medium to another, because its speed changes.

Light travels…SpeedBends
into a denser medium (air → water or glass)slows downtowards the normal
into a less dense medium (glass → air)speeds upaway from the normal
along the normal (at 90° to the surface)changesdoes not bend

Effects: a swimming pool looks shallower than it is, a pencil in water looks bent, lenses in spectacles and cameras focus light.

Dispersion: a prism splits white light into the colours of the spectrum because each colour bends by a different amount:

Red → Orange → Yellow → Green → Blue → Indigo → Violet (violet bends most)

topics.title: What is the impact of applications of radiation on society and the environment?
topics.html:
Visible light is one part of the electromagnetic spectrum:

Radio waves → Microwaves → Infrared → Visible light → Ultraviolet → X-rays → Gamma rays

RadiationUsesRisks
Radio wavesradio, TV, communicationgenerally low risk
Microwavesmicrowave ovens, mobile phones, satellitesheating of body tissue at high power
Infraredremote controls, thermal cameras, heatersburns from strong sources
Ultraviolet (UV)sterilising water and equipment, detecting fake notessunburn, skin cancer, eye damage. Use sunscreen and sunglasses
X-raysmedical imaging of bones, airport securitydamage to cells, so exposure is limited and staff wear lead aprons
Gamma rayscancer treatment, sterilising food and equipmentcan damage cells and cause cancer

Light pollution: too much artificial light at night disturbs animals (e.g. birds and turtles) and human sleep.

topics.title: How do advances in technology help in the understanding of cells?
topics.html:
• Cells are too small to see with the naked eye. The microscope made them visible
  • Robert Hooke (1665) saw tiny boxes in cork and named them "cells"
  • Cell theory: all living things are made of cells, the cell is the basic unit of life, and new cells come from existing cells
  • Electron microscopes magnify far more than light microscopes, showing tiny parts such as mitochondria in detail
Total magnification = eyepiece lens × objective lens   (e.g. 10× × 40× = 400×)
Microscope partJob
Eyepiecelens you look through
Objective lensesmain magnifying lenses (low, medium, high power)
Stage and clipshold the slide
Coarse and fine focus knobsbring the image into focus (use fine focus at high power)
Light source or mirrorshines light through the specimen
Watch out: always start with the lowest power objective lens, then switch to higher power.

topics.title: How can we use models to represent typical plant and animal cells?
topics.html:
PartJobPlantAnimal
Cell membranecontrols what enters and leaves the cell✓✓
Cytoplasmjelly where chemical reactions take place✓✓
Nucleuscontrols cell activities, contains genetic material (DNA)✓✓
Mitochondriarespiration takes place here, releasing energy✓✓
Cell wallmade of cellulose, gives the cell a fixed shape and support✓✗
Chloroplastscontain chlorophyll, absorb light for photosynthesis✓ (green parts only)✗
Vacuolestores cell sap and keeps the cell firmone large centralsmall, temporary
Specialised cellAdaptation
Red blood cellno nucleus and biconcave shape, so more room for haemoglobin to carry oxygen
Root hair celllong extension gives a large surface area to absorb water and minerals
Nerve celllong fibres carry messages around the body
Sperm celltail to swim, many mitochondria for energy
Guard cellsopen and close stomata to control gas exchange and water loss
Watch out: root cells have no chloroplasts because they get no light. "All plant cells have chloroplasts" is false.

topics.title: How does an organism function efficiently?
topics.html:
Cell → Tissue → Organ → Organ system → Organism

LevelMeaningHuman examplePlant example
Cellbasic unit of lifemuscle cellpalisade cell
Tissuegroup of similar cells doing one jobmuscle tissuexylem tissue
Organdifferent tissues working togetherheart, stomachleaf, root
Organ systemorgans working togethercirculatory, digestive systemshoot system
Organisma complete living thinghumanplant

Division of labour: different cells, tissues and organs are specialised for different jobs, so the organism works more efficiently than if every cell did everything.

topics.title: What is the particulate nature of matter?
topics.html:
Particulate model of matter:

  • All matter is made of tiny, discrete particles (atoms, molecules or ions)
  • There are spaces between the particles
  • The particles are in constant random motion
  • There are forces of attraction between the particles

Evidence:

  • Diffusion: the smell of perfume spreads across a room
  • Dissolving: sugar seems to disappear in water as its particles spread between water particles
  • Mixing 50 cm³ of alcohol with 50 cm³ of water gives less than 100 cm³, because the smaller particles fit into the spaces between the larger ones
  • Brownian motion: smoke or pollen grains jiggle randomly because invisible air or water particles hit them

topics.title: How can we explain the properties of different states of matter using the particulate nature of matter?
topics.html:
SolidLiquidGas
Arrangementclosely packed, regular patternclosely packed, irregularfar apart, random
Movementvibrate about fixed positionsslide past each othermove quickly in all directions
Forces between particlesvery strongstrongvery weak
Shapefixedtakes the shape of the containerfills the container
Volumefixedfixednot fixed
Compressible?nohardlyyes, large spaces between particles
ExampleWhy can a gas be compressed but a liquid cannot? Gas particles are far apart with large spaces, so they can be pushed closer together. Liquid particles are already closely packed.
Watch out: explain properties using particles: arrangement, spacing, movement and forces. "Solids are hard" alone scores nothing.

topics.title: How does the particulate nature of matter explain the behaviour of particles upon heating and cooling?
topics.html:
• Heating: particles gain energy and move or vibrate faster. They move further apart, so the substance expands
  • Cooling: particles lose energy, move slower and closer together, so the substance contracts
ChangeFrom → toParticle explanation
Meltingsolid → liquidparticles gain enough energy to overcome strong forces and leave fixed positions
Boiling / evaporationliquid → gasparticles gain enough energy to break free and move far apart
Condensationgas → liquidparticles lose energy, slow down and come closer together
Freezingliquid → solidparticles lose energy and settle into fixed positions
Sublimationsolid → gas directlye.g. dry ice, iodine
  • During melting and boiling the temperature stays constant, as energy goes into overcoming forces between particles (flat parts of a heating curve)
  • Boiling: at a fixed temperature, throughout the liquid, with bubbles. Evaporation: at any temperature, only at the surface
  • Evaporation is faster when it is hotter, windier, less humid, or the surface area is larger
Watch out: particles themselves do not expand or melt. They move faster and further apart.

topics.title: How does the particulate nature of matter help us appreciate other phenomena?
topics.html:
Diffusion: the net movement of particles from a region of higher concentration to lower concentration, caused by their random motion.

  • Fastest in gases, slower in liquids, almost none in solids
  • Faster at higher temperatures (particles move faster)
  • Lighter particles diffuse faster than heavier ones

Gas pressure: gas particles hit the walls of their container. Each collision pushes on the wall. Heating makes particles move faster and hit harder and more often, so pressure rises (e.g. tyres feel harder on a hot day, an aerosol can may burst if heated).

Other examples: wet clothes dry (evaporation), a dented ping-pong ball pops back in hot water (gas inside expands), a balloon shrinks in the fridge (gas contracts), salt dissolves faster in hot water.

Watch out: pressure comes from particles colliding with the walls, not from particles getting bigger.

topics.title: What is the simplest unit of an element and how do we represent its structure?
topics.html:
An atom is the smallest particle of an element that keeps its chemical properties.

ParticleChargeRelative massWhere
Proton+11nucleus
Neutron01nucleus
Electron−1≈ 1/1840 (almost 0)shells around the nucleus
  • The nucleus is tiny, holds almost all the mass and is positively charged. Most of an atom is empty space
  • A neutral atom has equal numbers of protons and electrons
  • Electrons fill shells in order: 2, 8, 8 (first 20 elements)

How the model changed: Dalton (solid sphere) → Thomson (electrons in a positive "pudding") → Rutherford (small, dense nucleus) → Bohr (electrons in shells). This shows scientific knowledge changes with new evidence.

ExampleSodium has 11 electrons: arrangement 2, 8, 1.

topics.title: How can the number of protons in an atom be used to identify an element?
topics.html:
• Proton number (atomic number): the number of protons. Every element has its own proton number, so it identifies the element
  • Nucleon number (mass number): protons + neutrons
  • The Periodic Table lists elements in order of proton number
Neutrons = nucleon number − proton number
ElementProton no.Nucleon no.pneElectron arrangement
Hydrogen111011
Carbon6126662, 4
Oxygen8168882, 6
Sodium11231112112, 8, 1
Chlorine17351718172, 8, 7

Isotopes: atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons (e.g. carbon-12 and carbon-14).

Watch out: the number of neutrons can vary, and electrons can be gained or lost, but if the number of protons changes, it becomes a different element.

topics.title: How do we represent the simplest units of elements and some compounds?
topics.html:
• A molecule is two or more atoms chemically joined together
  • Some elements exist as molecules of the same atoms: H₂, O₂, N₂, Cl₂ (diatomic)
  • Compounds are made of atoms of different elements joined together
  • A chemical formula shows which elements are present and how many atoms of each
SubstanceFormulaAtoms in one unit
Oxygen gasO₂2 oxygen
WaterH₂O2 hydrogen, 1 oxygen
Carbon dioxideCO₂1 carbon, 2 oxygen
MethaneCH₄1 carbon, 4 hydrogen
AmmoniaNH₃1 nitrogen, 3 hydrogen
Sodium chlorideNaClsodium and chlorine in a 1 : 1 ratio

A number in front counts whole molecules: 3H₂O means 3 water molecules, so 6 hydrogen atoms and 3 oxygen atoms.

Ions: charged particles formed when atoms lose electrons (positive ions, e.g. Na⁺) or gain electrons (negative ions, e.g. Cl⁻). Sodium chloride is made of ions, not molecules.

Watch out: the small number after a symbol applies only to the atom just before it. In CO₂ there is 1 carbon and 2 oxygen.

topics.title: What are some applications of atomic technologies and the possible issues that can arise from them?
topics.html:
ApplicationHow it is used
Nuclear powersplitting large atoms (nuclear fission) releases a lot of energy to generate electricity with little carbon dioxide
Medicineradiotherapy kills cancer cells. Radioactive tracers show how organs work. Gamma rays sterilise equipment
Carbon datingthe amount of carbon-14 left shows the age of ancient remains
Smoke detectors, food irradiationsmall radioactive sources detect smoke. Radiation kills bacteria in food
Possible issueDetails
Radiation exposuredamages living cells and can cause cancer
Nuclear accidentse.g. Chernobyl (1986) and Fukushima (2011) released radiation over large areas
Radioactive wastestays dangerous for thousands of years and must be stored safely
Weaponsthe same technology can be used to make nuclear weapons
Watch out: for "evaluate" questions, give a benefit and a risk, then a judgement with a reason.

topics.title: How do forces in nature affect us?
topics.html:
A force is a push or a pull. It is measured in newtons (N) with a spring balance (newton meter).

A force can:

  • start or stop an object moving
  • make a moving object speed up or slow down
  • change the direction of motion
  • change the shape or size of an object
Force in natureEffect on us
Gravitykeeps us on the ground, makes objects fall, holds the Moon in orbit, causes tides
Frictionlets us walk without slipping, lets vehicles brake
Wind (air pushing)moves sailboats and turns wind turbines, can damage buildings in storms
Water (moving water pushing)erodes riverbanks and coasts, turns water turbines
MagnetismEarth's magnetic field makes a compass point north
Watch out: a force cannot be seen. We only see its effects. Name the effect in your answer (e.g. "the ball changes direction").

topics.title: What are the types of forces?
topics.html:
Contact forces (objects touch)Non-contact forces (act at a distance)
Friction: opposes motion between surfaces in contactGravitational force: attraction between all masses
Air resistance / drag: friction from air or waterMagnetic force: between magnets, or magnets and iron/steel/nickel/cobalt
Normal (reaction) force: a surface pushing back on an objectElectrostatic force: between charged objects. Like charges repel, unlike attract
Tension: pull in a stretched rope or string
Upthrust: upward push from a liquid or gas

Mass vs weight

Weight = mass × gravitational field strength   W = mg
MassWeight
Meaningamount of matter in an objectgravitational pull on the object
Unitkilogram (kg)newton (N)
Measured withbeam or electronic balancespring balance
Changes on the Moon?NoYes, about 1/6 of Earth's

Friction: useful for walking, braking and gripping. A nuisance because it wastes energy as heat and wears parts out. Reduce it with lubricants (oil), ball bearings, smooth surfaces and streamlined shapes. Increase it with rough surfaces and tyre treads.

ExampleA 50 kg student on Earth (g = 10 N/kg): weight = 50 × 10 = 500 N.
Watch out: "My weight is 50 kg" is wrong in science. Mass is in kg, weight is in N.

topics.title: What happens when two or more objects interact?
topics.html:
• Forces always act in pairs. If A pushes B, B pushes back on A with an equal force in the opposite direction (e.g. a rocket pushes gas down, the gas pushes the rocket up)
  • When several forces act on one object, add them up to get the resultant force
ForcesResultantEffect
Balanced (equal and opposite)0 Nobject stays still, or keeps moving at the same speed in a straight line
Unbalancednot 0 Nobject speeds up, slows down or changes direction
Same direction: add  ·  Opposite directions: subtract (bigger − smaller), direction of the bigger force
ExampleA box is pushed right with 30 N and friction acts left with 10 N. Resultant = 30 − 10 = 20 N to the right, so the box speeds up to the right.
ExampleA skydiver at steady speed: weight (down) = air resistance (up). Forces are balanced, so speed stays constant.
Watch out: balanced forces do not mean the object is still. It can be moving at a steady speed. Always give the direction of a resultant force.

topics.title: How is energy conserved?
topics.html:
Principle of conservation of energy: energy cannot be created or destroyed. It can only be converted from one form to another. The total amount stays the same.

FormExample
Kineticmoving car, flowing water
Gravitational potentialbook on a high shelf, water in a dam
Elastic potentialstretched rubber band, compressed spring
Chemical potentialfood, fuel, batteries
Electrical, light, sound, thermal (heat), nuclearcurrent in wires, lamp, speaker, hot drink, Sun's core

Energy conversions:

Torch: chemical → electrical → light + heat

Falling ball: gravitational potential → kinetic (→ heat and sound on hitting the ground)

Pendulum: gravitational potential ⇄ kinetic

Work done = force × distance moved in the direction of the force   W = F × d  (J)
Power = energy converted ÷ time   P = Et  (W = J/s)

In real machines some energy is always converted to wasted forms (usually heat and sound), so the useful output is less than the input. The energy is not lost, just not useful.

ExampleLifting a 20 N bag up 1.5 m: W = 20 × 1.5 = 30 J. Done in 3 s: P = 30 ÷ 3 = 10 W.
Watch out: "energy is used up" or "lost" is wrong. Say energy is converted to heat or sound that spreads to the surroundings.

topics.title: What are the sources of energy that we use?
topics.html:
RenewableNon-renewable
Meaningreplaced naturally and will not run outlimited, takes millions of years to form, will run out
Examplessolar, wind, hydroelectric, tidal, geothermal, biomassfossil fuels (coal, oil, natural gas), nuclear fuel (uranium)
SourceAdvantageDisadvantage
Fossil fuelsreliable, large amounts of energy, power stations easy to controlrelease carbon dioxide (global warming) and air pollutants, will run out
Solarclean, free once installedonly works in daylight, affected by cloud, needs large area
Windclean, no fuel costdepends on wind, noisy, needs space
Hydroelectricclean, reliabledams flood land and destroy habitats
Nuclearhuge energy from little fuel, no carbon dioxide while runningradioactive waste, risk of accidents
Biomassuses waste, renewableburning releases carbon dioxide, uses land

Singapore: most electricity is generated from imported natural gas. With little land and weak winds, solar is the main renewable source (e.g. solar panels on HDB rooftops and floating solar farms on reservoirs).

Most energy comes from the Sun: Sun → plants (photosynthesis) → fossil fuels / food

Watch out: nuclear energy is non-renewable (uranium runs out), even though it produces little carbon dioxide.

topics.title: What does a change in temperature indicate?
topics.html:
TemperatureHeat
Meaninghow hot or cold something is. A measure of the average kinetic energy of its particlesenergy transferred from a hotter to a colder region because of a temperature difference
Unitdegree Celsius (°C) or kelvin (K)joule (J)
Measured withthermometer, temperature sensorcalculated, not measured directly
  • Temperature rises: the object gains heat, so its particles move faster
  • Temperature falls: the object loses heat, so its particles move slower
  • Heat flows from hot to cold until both reach the same temperature (thermal equilibrium)
  • A bigger object at the same temperature has more heat energy (more particles), e.g. a bathtub of warm water holds more heat than a cup at the same temperature

Reference points: ice melts at 0 °C, water boils at 100 °C (at normal pressure), human body about 37 °C.

Watch out: heat and temperature are not the same. "The temperature of the soup is 300 J" is wrong.

topics.title: What effects does heat transfer have on an object?
topics.html:
1. Expansion and contraction

  • Heated: particles vibrate or move faster and further apart, so the object expands. Cooled: it contracts
  • Gases expand most, then liquids, then solids
Use or problemExplanation
Gaps in railway tracks and bridgesleave room to expand on hot days so they don't buckle
Overhead cables sag in hot weatherthey expand and get longer
Liquid-in-glass thermometerliquid expands up the narrow tube when heated
Bimetallic strip (fire alarm, thermostat)two metals expand by different amounts, so the strip bends
Hot water loosens a tight metal lidthe metal lid expands more than the glass jar

2. Change of state

Solid ⇄ Liquid ⇄ Gas   (melting / freezing, boiling or evaporation / condensation)

  • Gaining heat: melting, boiling, evaporation, sublimation. Losing heat: freezing, condensation
  • Temperature stays constant during melting and boiling. The heat is used to break the forces between particles
  • Boiling happens at a fixed temperature throughout the liquid. Evaporation happens at any temperature, only at the surface
Watch out: particles do not expand. The spaces between them get bigger.

topics.title: How does the transfer of heat energy occur?
topics.html:
MethodHow it worksHappens in
Conductionvibrating particles pass energy to neighbouring particles. In metals, free electrons also carry energy, so metals conduct fastmainly solids
Convectionthe heated fluid expands, becomes less dense and rises. Cooler, denser fluid sinks to take its place, forming a convection currentliquids and gases only
Radiationenergy travels as infrared waves. No particles neededeverywhere, including a vacuum (how the Sun's heat reaches Earth)
  • Good conductors: metals (copper, aluminium, iron). Insulators (poor conductors): plastic, wood, glass, air, wool, polystyrene
  • Materials that trap air (wool, feathers, foam) are good insulators because air is a poor conductor and trapped air cannot form convection currents
  • Convection examples: heater near the floor, air-conditioner near the ceiling, sea and land breezes, heating water in a kettle from the bottom
Example: sea breeze (day)Land heats up faster than the sea. Air above the land is heated, expands and rises. Cooler air from over the sea moves in to replace it.
Watch out: convection cannot happen in solids because their particles cannot move from place to place. Never write "heat rises". Say "hot air rises because it is less dense".

topics.title: What affects the rate at which heat energy is transferred?
topics.html:
FactorFaster transfer when…
Temperature differencethe difference between object and surroundings is larger
Surface areaexposed surface area is larger (e.g. fins on a motorbike engine, spreading out hot food)
Materialthe material is a good conductor (metal) rather than an insulator
Thicknessthe material is thinner
Surface colour and texture (radiation)the surface is dull and black (good absorber and emitter). Shiny and white surfaces are poor absorbers and emitters, and reflect radiation
Movement of air or liquidair or liquid flows over the surface (e.g. fan, stirring)
Investigation tipTo test one factor (e.g. colour), keep everything else the same: same volume of water, same starting temperature, same can size, same time. Record temperature every minute.
Watch out: in an experiment question, name the variable you change, the one you measure, and at least two you keep constant.

topics.title: How can we harness heat transfer in daily life?
topics.html:
ApplicationHow it uses heat transfer
Cooking potmetal base (good conductor) heats food fast. Plastic or wooden handle (insulator) is safe to hold
Vacuum flaskvacuum stops conduction and convection. Silvered walls reflect radiation. Stopper prevents convection and evaporation
Solar water heaterblack pipes or panels absorb radiation from the Sun
Buildings in Singaporelight-coloured roofs reflect radiation, ventilation and high ceilings let hot air rise and escape, greenery shades walls
Refrigeratorfreezing unit at the top so cold air sinks and sets up convection currents
Double-glazed windowstrapped air or vacuum between panes reduces conduction
Cooler box, polystyrene cupinsulating material with trapped air reduces conduction
Clothinglight colours in hot weather reflect radiation. Layers trap air to keep warm in cold places
Watch out: explain each feature with the method it controls: "the vacuum prevents heat loss by conduction and convection because there are no particles".

topics.title: How do we identify a chemical change?
topics.html:
Physical changeChemical change
New substance formed?NoYes
Reversible?usually easily reversedusually not easily reversed
Energy changesmalloften large (heat or light given out or taken in)
Examplesmelting ice, dissolving sugar, cutting paper, boiling waterburning paper, rusting, cooking an egg, baking a cake, fruit ripening

Signs that a chemical change may have happened:

  • colour change (e.g. iron turning reddish-brown)
  • gas given off: bubbles or fizzing (effervescence)
  • a precipitate (insoluble solid) forms when two solutions are mixed
  • temperature change: gets hot or cold
  • light or sound produced
  • change in smell
Watch out: signs only suggest a chemical change. Boiling water also gives off bubbles but no new substance forms. The only proof is a new substance.

topics.title: What are the different types of chemical changes?
topics.html:
TypeWhat happensExample (word equation)
Combustion (burning)a substance reacts with oxygen, giving out heat and lightmethane + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water
Oxidationa substance combines with oxygen, often slowlyiron + oxygen + water → rust (hydrated iron(III) oxide)
Thermal decompositionheat breaks one substance into simpler onescalcium carbonate → calcium oxide + carbon dioxide
Neutralisationan acid reacts with an alkali or basehydrochloric acid + sodium hydroxide → sodium chloride + water
Metal + acida reactive metal reacts with a dilute acidmagnesium + hydrochloric acid → magnesium chloride + hydrogen
Carbonate + acidgives off carbon dioxide (fizzing)calcium carbonate + hydrochloric acid → calcium chloride + water + carbon dioxide
Reaction caused by lightlight energy drives the changephotosynthesis: carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen
Electrolysiselectricity breaks down a compoundwater → hydrogen + oxygen
Gas testResult
Hydrogen: lighted splint"pop" sound
Oxygen: glowing splintrelights
Carbon dioxide: bubble through limewaterwhite precipitate (limewater turns chalky)
Watch out: rusting needs both oxygen and water. Iron in dry air or in boiled water with an oil layer does not rust.

topics.title: How do chemical changes occur?
topics.html:
• In a chemical change, the atoms in the reactants are rearranged to form new products. Bonds between atoms are broken and new bonds are formed
  • No atoms are created or destroyed, so the total mass stays the same (conservation of mass). In an open container, mass may seem to drop if a gas escapes
  • Reactions need particles to collide. They happen faster with higher temperature, higher concentration, smaller pieces (larger surface area) or a catalyst
reactants → products
Energy changeMeaningExamples
Exothermicgives out heat, surroundings get warmercombustion, neutralisation, respiration, hand warmers
Endothermictakes in heat, surroundings get colderthermal decomposition, photosynthesis, instant cold packs

Writing equations: word equation first, then a balanced chemical equation by counting atoms on both sides. Only change the numbers in front.

2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO    CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O
Watch out: never change the small numbers inside a formula when balancing. H₂O must stay H₂O.

topics.title: How does knowledge of chemical reactions help us in daily life?
topics.html:
UseChemistry behind it
Preventing rustpaint, oil or grease, plastic coating keep out oxygen and water. Galvanising (zinc coating) protects iron even when scratched
Preserving foodrefrigeration slows reactions. Vacuum packing and canning remove oxygen. Antioxidants slow oxidation (e.g. lemon juice stops cut apples browning)
Fire safetyfire needs fuel, oxygen and heat (the fire triangle). Remove one to put it out: fire blanket or CO₂ extinguisher removes oxygen, water removes heat
Antacidsa base neutralises excess stomach acid
Bakingbaking powder (sodium hydrogencarbonate) releases carbon dioxide when heated, making cakes rise
Fuelscombustion releases energy for cooking, transport and electricity
Treating acidic soilfarmers add lime (a base) to neutralise it
Watch out: never use water on an oil or electrical fire. Water spreads burning oil and conducts electricity.

topics.title: How do our actions impact the environment?
topics.html:
Human actionImpact
Deforestation (for farms, timber, buildings)habitat loss and extinction, soil erosion, less carbon dioxide absorbed
Burning fossil fuelsmore carbon dioxide → enhanced greenhouse effect → global warming, rising sea levels. Air pollution and haze
Water pollution (sewage, fertilisers, oil, waste)fertiliser runoff causes algae to grow fast. When algae die, decomposers use up oxygen and fish die
Land pollution (plastic, litter)animals eat or get trapped in plastic. Microplastics enter food chains
Overfishing, huntingpopulations fall faster than they can recover. Food webs are disrupted
Introducing foreign (invasive) speciesthey compete with or eat native species

Positive actions: conservation, reforestation, recycling, using renewable energy. See 12.5.

Watch out: link each action to a specific effect on organisms ("fewer trees → fewer habitats → fewer animals"), not just "it is bad for the environment".

topics.title: How does an environment influence the survival of organisms?
topics.html:
• Environment: the surroundings of an organism, made up of biotic (living: plants, animals, microorganisms) and abiotic (non-living) factors
  • Abiotic factors: light, temperature, water, air (oxygen, carbon dioxide), soil pH and minerals, salinity (saltiness)
  • Habitat: the place where an organism lives
  • Adaptation: a feature that helps an organism survive in its environment
OrganismAdaptationHow it helps
Cactus (desert)spines instead of leaves, thick waxy stem, long rootsreduce water loss, store water, reach water deep underground
Camelhump stores fat, long eyelashes, wide feetenergy and water when food is scarce, keeps sand out, walks on sand
Mangrove trees (Singapore coasts)breathing roots (pneumatophores) stick up out of mud. Prop rootstake in oxygen from air in waterlogged mud. Support in soft mud
Polar bearthick fur and fat, white coatinsulation, camouflage in snow
Owllarge eyes, active at nightsees in low light, hunts when prey is active

Structural adaptations are body features. Behavioural adaptations are actions (e.g. animals sheltering in the heat of the day, migration).

Watch out: state the feature and explain how it helps survival. "The cactus has spines" alone scores half.

topics.title: What types of interactions affect the stability of an ecosystem?
topics.html:
InteractionWho benefitsExample
Predator–preypredator gains, prey is killedeagle and snake, lion and zebra
Competitionboth are harmed (less resource for each)plants competing for light and water. Animals for food, mates, space
Mutualismboth benefit (+ +)bee and flower (nectar / pollination), clownfish and sea anemone
Commensalismone benefits, the other is unaffected (+ 0)barnacles on a whale, orchid growing on a tree
Parasitismparasite benefits, host is harmed (+ −)tick or flea on a dog, tapeworm in a human

Predator–prey cycle: more prey → more food → predator numbers rise → more prey eaten → prey numbers fall → predators starve → predator numbers fall → prey recover. The predator graph peaks after the prey graph.

These interactions keep population sizes in check, which keeps the ecosystem stable.

Watch out: commensalism and mutualism are often mixed up. Ask: does the second organism gain anything? If not, it's commensalism.

topics.title: What are the processes involved in maintaining a stable ecosystem?
topics.html:
1. Energy flow through food chains and webs

Sun → Producer → Primary consumer → Secondary consumer → Tertiary consumer

  • Producers (green plants) make food by photosynthesis. Consumers eat other organisms. Decomposers (bacteria, fungi) break down dead matter and waste
  • Arrows show the direction of energy flow: from the organism eaten to the eater
  • Only about 10% of energy passes to the next level. The rest is lost as heat (respiration), movement and waste. So food chains are short and there are fewer organisms at higher levels
  • A food web is many linked food chains. More links make an ecosystem more stable

2. Cycling of nutrients: the carbon cycle

Removes CO₂ from airAdds CO₂ to air
photosynthesis by plantsrespiration by all living things, combustion of fuels, decomposition by decomposers
Photosynthesis: carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen  (light, chlorophyll)
Respiration: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + energy
ExampleIn a food web, if snakes are removed, frogs increase (fewer eaten), so insects decrease (more eaten by frogs).
Watch out: energy flows one way and is not recycled. Nutrients like carbon are recycled.

topics.title: How can we help to maintain a stable ecosystem?
topics.html:
ActionHow it helpsExample
Protect habitatskeeps food webs complete and species safeCentral Catchment and Bukit Timah Nature Reserves, Sungei Buloh Wetland Reserve
Replant and restorecreates habitats and absorbs carbon dioxidemangrove replanting, OneMillionTrees movement
Reduce, reuse, recycleless waste and pollution, fewer resources usedbring own bag and bottle, recycling bins
Save energy, use renewablesless carbon dioxide from burning fossil fuelssolar panels, switching off appliances
Sustainable fishing and farmingpopulations can recoverfishing quotas, buying certified seafood
Laws and educationstop illegal hunting, trade and dumpingbans on wildlife trade, campaigns
Watch out: say how the action helps the ecosystem, e.g. "recycling paper means fewer trees are cut down, so habitats are kept".

topics.title: What does an electrical system comprise?
topics.html:
PartJobExamples
Sourceprovides electrical energy (pushes the current)cell, battery, mains supply, solar panel
Conductorcarries current between componentscopper wires
Loadconverts electrical energy to other formsbulb, motor, buzzer, heater
Switchopens or closes the circuitpush switch, light switch

Current only flows in a closed circuit (a complete loop with no gaps).

QuantityMeaningUnitMeasured with
Current Irate of flow of electric chargeampere (A)ammeter, connected in series
Voltage Velectrical "push" from the source, or energy used by a componentvolt (V)voltmeter, connected in parallel
Resistance Rhow much a component opposes currentohm (Ω)calculated: R = V ÷ I
Power Prate of converting electrical energywatt (W)calculated: P = V × I (see 13.4)
SeriesParallel
Layoutone looptwo or more branches
Currentsame everywheresplits between branches, adds up to the total
Voltageshared between componentssame across each branch
One bulb blowsall go outothers stay on (used in homes)

Conventional current flows from the positive (+, long line) to the negative (−, short line) terminal. Electrons actually flow the other way.

Watch out: ammeter in series, voltmeter in parallel. Swapping them is a common lost mark in circuit diagrams.

topics.title: How do electrical components affect the output of an electrical system?
topics.html:
Marked optional for G2 Science in the textbook.

V = I × R   (voltage = current × resistance)
ChangeEffect on currentEffect on output
Add more cells in seriesincreasesbulbs brighter, motor faster
Add more bulbs in seriesdecreases (more resistance)each bulb dimmer
Add more bulbs in paralleltotal current increaseseach bulb as bright as one on its own (battery runs down faster)
Increase resistance (e.g. variable resistor)decreasesbulb dimmer, motor slower

Resistance of a wire is higher when it is: longer, thinner, made of a poorer conductor (e.g. nichrome rather than copper), or hotter.

A variable resistor (rheostat) changes resistance to control the output, e.g. a dimmer switch or a fan speed control.

ExampleA bulb has 3 V across it and a current of 0.5 A. R = 3 ÷ 0.5 = 6 Ω.
A 12 V supply drives current through a 4 Ω resistor. I = 12 ÷ 4 = 3 A.
Watch out: rearrange the formula before substituting, and always write the unit (A, V or Ω).

topics.title: Total resistance in series and parallel circuits
topics.html:
How to find the total (effective) resistance of several resistors, and why the formulas work. Every step uses only V = I × R.

Series: same current through every resistor

  1. Each resistor: V₁ = IR₁,  V₂ = IR₂,  V₃ = IR₃
  2. The voltages share the supply: V = V₁ + V₂ + V₃ = I(R₁ + R₂ + R₃)
  3. For the whole circuit, V = I × Rtotal, so
Rtotal = R₁ + R₂ + R₃

Parallel: same voltage across every branch

  1. Each branch has the full supply voltage: V₁ = V₂ = V₃ = V
  2. Each branch current: I₁ = VR₁,  I₂ = VR₂,  I₃ = VR₃
  3. The currents add up: Itotal = I₁ + I₂ + I₃
  4. Rtotal = VItotal = VVR₁ + VR₂ + VR₃
  5. Flip both sides and divide through by V:
1Rtotal = 1R₁ + 1R₂ + 1R₃

Shortcut for two resistors in parallel: Rtotal = R₁ × R₂R₁ + R₂ (product over sum)

SeriesParallel
Currentsame everywhere: Iadds up: Itotal = I₁ + I₂ + I₃
Voltageadds up: V = V₁ + V₂ + V₃same across each branch: V
Total resistanceR₁ + R₂ + R₃ (bigger than any one)1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + 1/R₃ (smaller than the smallest)
Example 1: series2 Ω, 3 Ω and 5 Ω in series with a 12 V supply.
Rtotal = 2 + 3 + 5 = 10 Ω.  I = 12 ÷ 10 = 1.2 A.
V₁ = 1.2 × 2 = 2.4 V,  V₂ = 1.2 × 3 = 3.6 V,  V₃ = 1.2 × 5 = 6.0 V. Check: 2.4 + 3.6 + 6.0 = 12 V ✓
Example 2: two in parallel6 Ω and 3 Ω in parallel with a 6 V supply.
1/R = 1/6 + 1/3 = 1/6 + 2/6 = 3/6, so Rtotal = 2 Ω (shortcut: 18 ÷ 9 = 2 Ω).
I₁ = 6 ÷ 6 = 1 A,  I₂ = 6 ÷ 3 = 2 A,  Itotal = 3 A. Check: 6 V ÷ 2 Ω = 3 A ✓
Example 3: three in parallel2 Ω, 3 Ω and 6 Ω in parallel.
1/R = 1/2 + 1/3 + 1/6 = 3/6 + 2/6 + 1/6 = 6/6 = 1, so Rtotal = 1 Ω.
Watch out: in parallel, 1/Rtotal is not the answer. Remember to flip it at the end (1/R = 3/6 means R = 2 Ω, not 0.5 Ω). Check: the parallel total must be smaller than the smallest resistor.

topics.title: What are some benefits and risks associated with the applications of electrical systems?
topics.html:
Benefits: lighting, cooking and heating, refrigeration of food and medicine, communication (phones, internet), transport (MRT, electric buses), medical equipment, entertainment.

RiskCause
Electric shocktouching live wires, damaged insulation, wet hands or water near appliances
Fireoverloading a socket (too many appliances), short circuit, wires overheating
Short circuitcurrent takes a path with almost no resistance, so a very large current flows and wires overheat
Safety featureHow it protects
Fuse (in the live wire)thin wire melts when current is too large, breaking the circuit
Circuit breakerswitch that trips off automatically when current is too large. Can be reset
Earth wireif a live wire touches a metal casing, current flows safely to earth instead of through the user, and the fuse blows
Insulation / double insulationplastic covering stops users touching live parts
Wire in a 3-pin plugColour
Livebrown
Neutralblue
Earthgreen and yellow stripes
Watch out: the fuse and switch must be on the live wire, so the appliance is disconnected from the high voltage when they break the circuit.

topics.title: How do we reduce the consumption of electrical energy?
topics.html:
Finding power from voltage and current

Power is how fast an appliance converts electrical energy, measured in watts (W). 1 W = 1 joule per second.

Power = voltage × current   P = V × I
watts (W) = volts (V) × amperes (A)
To findUse
PowerP = V × I
CurrentI = P ÷ V
VoltageV = P ÷ I

Steps: (1) write the formula, (2) substitute the values, (3) calculate, (4) give the unit.

Example 1: find powerA kettle on Singapore's 230 V mains draws a current of 8 A.
P = V × I = 230 × 8 = 1840 W (1.84 kW).
Example 2: find currentA 2300 W air-conditioner runs on 230 V.
I = P ÷ V = 2300 ÷ 230 = 10 A.
Example 3: torch bulbA bulb has 3 V across it and 0.5 A through it.
P = 3 × 0.5 = 1.5 W.
Example 4: power, then energy and costA 230 V heater draws 5 A for 2 hours at $0.30 per kWh.
P = 230 × 5 = 1150 W = 1.15 kW.
Energy = 1.15 kW × 2 h = 2.3 kWh.
Cost = 2.3 × $0.30 = $0.69.

Choosing a fuse: work out the normal current with I = P ÷ V, then pick the fuse rated just above it. A 1840 W kettle draws 8 A, so use a 13 A fuse, not a 3 A or 5 A fuse.

Linking with V = IR: if you know the current and resistance, first find the voltage (V = I × R), then the power (P = V × I).

Watch out: current must be in amperes. Convert mA first (250 mA = 0.25 A). And kW ≠ W: divide by 1000 before working out kWh.

Energy used and its cost

Energy (kWh) = Power (kW) × time (h)
Cost = energy used (kWh) × price per kWh
ExampleA 2000 W air-conditioner runs 5 h a day. Energy = 2 kW × 5 h = 10 kWh per day. At $0.30 per kWh, it costs $3.00 a day, or about $90 a month.

Ways to save electricity:

  • Switch off lights and appliances when not in use, including at the wall socket (standby still uses power)
  • Use LED bulbs: they convert more energy to light and less to heat than older bulbs
  • Buy appliances with more ticks on the Energy Label: more ticks means more energy efficient
  • Set the air-conditioner to 25 °C or higher, or use a fan instead
  • Use natural light and ventilation, and keep fridge doors closed

Why it matters: most electricity in Singapore comes from burning natural gas, which releases carbon dioxide. Using less electricity lowers both the bill and emissions.

Watch out: convert W to kW (÷ 1000) and minutes to hours (÷ 60) before calculating kWh.

topics.title: Why is a digestive system needed in humans?
topics.html:
Most food molecules (starch, proteins, fats) are large and insoluble. They cannot pass through the gut wall into the blood. Digestion breaks them down into small, soluble molecules that can be absorbed and used by cells.

TypeWhat happensExamples
Physical digestionbreaks food into smaller pieces, increasing surface area for enzymes. No new substancechewing by teeth, churning in stomach, bile emulsifying fats
Chemical digestionenzymes break large molecules into small onesamylase breaking starch into maltose
NutrientBroken down into
Starch (carbohydrate)glucose
Proteinamino acids
Fatsfatty acids and glycerol

Vitamins, minerals and water are already small and are absorbed without digestion. Fibre is not digested but helps food move through the gut.

Food testReagentPositive result
Starchiodine solutionbrown → blue-black
Reducing sugarBenedict's solution, heatedblue → brick-red precipitate
Proteinbiuret solutionblue → violet
Fatsethanol, then waterwhite emulsion
Watch out: the reason for digestion is size and solubility. Mention both.

topics.title: How do the parts of the human digestive system work together?
topics.html:
Mouth → Oesophagus → Stomach → Small intestine → Large intestine → Rectum → Anus

PartWhat happens
Mouthteeth chew food. Saliva moistens it and contains amylase (starch → maltose)
Oesophagusperistalsis: waves of muscle contraction push food to the stomach
Stomachchurns food. Hydrochloric acid kills bacteria and gives the right pH for protease (protein digestion starts)
Liver and gall bladderliver makes bile, stored in the gall bladder. Bile emulsifies fats into tiny droplets
Pancreasreleases pancreatic juice with amylase, protease and lipase into the small intestine
Small intestinedigestion is completed. Digested food is absorbed into the blood through villi
Large intestineabsorbs water and minerals. Forms faeces
Rectum, anusstores faeces, then removes them (egestion)
EnzymeSubstrate → productWhere
Amylasestarch → maltosemouth, small intestine
Maltasemaltose → glucosesmall intestine
Proteaseprotein → amino acidsstomach, small intestine
Lipasefats → fatty acids + glycerolsmall intestine

Villi are adapted for absorption: they give a very large surface area, have walls one cell thick, and contain many blood capillaries.

Enzymes: proteins that speed up reactions. Each works on one substance (lock and key). They work best at an optimum temperature (about 37 °C in humans) and pH, and are denatured at high temperatures.

Watch out: bile is not an enzyme. It breaks fat into droplets physically, which gives lipase a larger surface area to work on.

topics.title: How do the end products of digestion affect the body?
topics.html:
After absorption, the end products are carried in the blood to every cell and used there (assimilation).

End productUse in the bodyIf in excess
Glucoseused in respiration to release energystored as glycogen in the liver and muscles, or converted to fat
Amino acidsbuild new proteins for growth and repair, enzymes, hormonesbroken down in the liver. The waste (urea) is removed by the kidneys
Fatty acids and glycerolmake cell membranes, energy store, insulation, protect organsstored as fat under the skin and around organs
Aerobic respiration: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + energy
Watch out: respiration releases energy in cells. It is not the same as breathing, which moves air in and out of the lungs.

topics.title: What are some issues that affect the human digestive system?
topics.html:
IssueCausePrevention or care
Constipationtoo little fibre and water, so faeces become hardeat vegetables, fruit, wholegrains, drink water
Diarrhoeainfection from contaminated food or water. Large intestine absorbs too little waterwash hands, eat clean food, drink fluids to avoid dehydration
Gastric ulcer, gastritisstomach lining damaged by bacteria, too much acid, some painkillers, irregular mealsregular meals, medical treatment
Tooth decaybacteria feed on sugar and produce acid that dissolves enamelbrush twice a day, less sugary food and drinks
Obesitytaking in more energy than the body usesbalanced diet, regular exercise

A balanced diet has the right amounts of carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals, fibre and water (e.g. Singapore's "My Healthy Plate": half fruit and vegetables, a quarter wholegrains, a quarter protein).

Watch out: link the cause to the part of the gut affected, e.g. "too little water is absorbed in the large intestine, so faeces are watery".

topics.title: What are the functions of a transport system and its parts?
topics.html:
A transport system carries useful substances (oxygen, food, water) to cells and removes waste (carbon dioxide, urea) from them.

Humans: heart, blood vessels and blood

Vena cava → Right atrium → Right ventricle → Pulmonary artery → Lungs → Pulmonary vein → Left atrium → Left ventricle → Aorta → Body

  • Right side pumps deoxygenated blood to the lungs. Left side pumps oxygenated blood to the body
  • The left ventricle has the thickest wall because it pumps blood all round the body. Valves stop blood flowing backwards
VesselDirectionFeatures
Arteryaway from heartthick, muscular, elastic wall. High pressure
Veintowards heartthin wall, wide space inside, valves. Low pressure
Capillarylinks arteries and veinswall one cell thick so substances pass in and out
Blood partJob
Red blood cellscarry oxygen using haemoglobin. No nucleus, biconcave shape for more space and surface area
White blood cellsfight germs (engulf them or make antibodies)
Plateletshelp blood clot at wounds
Plasmaliquid that carries dissolved food, carbon dioxide, hormones and urea

Plants: xylem carries water and mineral salts up from the roots (one direction). Phloem carries sugars made in the leaves to all parts (up and down). Transpiration (water evaporating from leaves through stomata) pulls water up the xylem. It is faster when it is hot, windy, bright or dry.

Watch out: the pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood. Arteries are named by direction (away from the heart), not by oxygen.

topics.title: What are the processes involved in the movement of substances in and out of cells?
topics.html:
DiffusionOsmosis
Definitionnet movement of particles from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentrationnet movement of water molecules from a dilute solution (more water) to a concentrated solution (less water) through a partially permeable membrane
What movesany particles (gases, dissolved substances)water only
Examplesoxygen from air sacs into blood in the lungs. Carbon dioxide into a leaf. Digested food into villiroot hair cells taking in water from soil. Water moving between plant cells

Diffusion is faster when: the concentration difference is larger, the temperature is higher, the surface area is larger, or the distance is shorter.

Cell placed inPlant cellRed blood cell (animal)
Pure water (dilute)gains water, becomes firm (turgid). Cell wall stops it burstinggains water, swells and bursts
Concentrated salt or sugar solutionloses water, becomes limp (flaccid). Plant wiltsloses water and shrinks
ExampleSalted cucumber slices go soft: water leaves the cucumber cells by osmosis into the more concentrated salt solution outside.
Watch out: in osmosis, describe water moving, not salt or sugar. And always mention the partially permeable membrane.

topics.title: What issues arise when parts of the human transport system do not work well?
topics.html:
IssueWhat happensEffect
Coronary heart diseasefatty deposits build up inside the coronary arteries that supply the heart muscle, narrowing themless oxygen reaches heart muscle, causing chest pain. A blocked artery causes a heart attack
High blood pressureblood pushes too hard on artery wallsdamages arteries, raises risk of heart attack and stroke
Strokeblood supply to part of the brain is blocked or a vessel burstsbrain cells die, can cause paralysis or speech problems
Anaemiatoo little haemoglobin or too few red blood cells, often from lack of ironless oxygen carried, so tiredness and paleness
Faulty heart valvesvalves don't close properly, so blood flows backwardsheart pumps less efficiently

Risk factors: smoking, diet high in saturated fat and salt, lack of exercise, obesity, stress, family history.

Prevention: do not smoke, eat less fatty and salty food, exercise regularly, keep a healthy weight, have health check-ups.

Treatment: medicines, a stent (small tube that holds an artery open), bypass surgery, pacemaker or heart valve replacement.

Watch out: the coronary arteries supply blood to the heart muscle itself, not the blood inside the heart chambers.

topics.title: What is the function of the human sexual reproductive system?
topics.html:
• Function: to produce offspring, so the human species continues
  • Sexual reproduction involves two parents. A male gamete (sperm) fuses with a female gamete (egg or ovum). This is fertilisation
  • Offspring get genetic material from both parents, so they show variation (they are not identical)

The system: produces gametes, produces sex hormones (testosterone in males, oestrogen and progesterone in females), allows sperm to meet the egg, and (in females) protects and nourishes the developing baby.

Puberty is when the reproductive organs mature and secondary sexual characteristics develop, controlled by sex hormones.

SpermEgg
Made intestesovaries
Sizevery smallmuch larger (contains food store)
Moves?yes, swims with a tailno, moved along the oviduct by cilia
Numbermillions producedusually one released per month

topics.title: How do the parts of each reproductive system work together?
topics.html:
Male organJob
Testesproduce sperm and testosterone
Scrotumholds the testes outside the body, at a slightly lower temperature for sperm production
Sperm ductcarries sperm from the testes to the urethra
Prostate gland, seminal vesicleadd fluid that nourishes sperm and helps them swim (sperm + fluid = semen)
Urethra, peniscarry semen out of the body
Female organJob
Ovariesrelease an egg about once a month. Produce oestrogen and progesterone
Oviduct (fallopian tube)carries the egg to the uterus. Fertilisation happens here
Uterusembryo implants in its thick lining and the fetus develops
Cervixring of muscle at the neck of the uterus
Vaginareceives sperm. Birth canal

Sperm + egg → zygote (in oviduct) → divides into an embryo → implants in uterus lining → fetus → birth (about 9 months)

  • Placenta: food and oxygen pass from mother to fetus. Carbon dioxide and wastes pass from fetus to mother. Their blood does not mix
  • Umbilical cord: connects the fetus to the placenta
  • Amniotic fluid: cushions the fetus from bumps
  • Menstrual cycle (about 28 days): days 1–5 menstruation (uterus lining breaks down). Lining thickens again. Ovulation (egg released) around day 14. Fertile period about days 11–17
Watch out: fertilisation happens in the oviduct. The uterus is where implantation happens.

topics.title: How can the function of the human reproductive system be disrupted?
topics.html:
DisruptionDetails
Sexually transmitted infections (STIs)spread through sexual contact. Examples: HIV (attacks the immune system and can lead to AIDS), syphilis and gonorrhoea (bacterial). Some can damage reproductive organs and cause infertility
Infertilityunable to conceive, e.g. blocked oviducts, egg not released, low sperm count or sperm that swim poorly
Harmful substances in pregnancysmoking, alcohol and drugs cross the placenta and can cause low birth weight, birth defects or miscarriage
Hormone imbalancecan stop ovulation or sperm production
Agefertility falls as people get older

Preventing STIs: abstinence is the only certain way. Condoms reduce the risk. Some STIs can spread by sharing needles, by blood, or from mother to baby.

Watch out: antibiotics treat bacterial STIs like syphilis and gonorrhoea, but not HIV, which is a virus.

topics.title: How do medical advancements impact human reproduction and survival?
topics.html:
AdvancementHow it helpsIssue to consider
In vitro fertilisation (IVF)eggs are fertilised by sperm outside the body, and an embryo is placed in the uterus. Helps infertile couplesexpensive, may need several attempts, raises ethical questions about unused embryos
Contraceptionprevents pregnancy, so families can plan. Barrier methods (condoms) stop sperm reaching the egg. Hormonal methods (pills) stop ovulation. Surgical methods (cutting the sperm ducts or oviducts) are permanentno method is 100% effective. Only condoms reduce STI risk
Ultrasound scans and prenatal testscheck the fetus's growth and detect problems earlyresults can lead to difficult decisions
Vaccinese.g. the HPV vaccine protects against a virus that can cause cervical cancermust be given before exposure
Medicines for STIsantibiotics cure bacterial STIs. Antiretroviral drugs control HIV so people can live longer, healthier livesHIV has no cure yet
Watch out: "evaluate" questions want a benefit and a limitation or ethical issue, then a judgement.

topics.title: Acids & alkalis
topics.html:
0714
strong acidneutralstrong alkali
  • Litmus: acid turns blue litmus red. Alkali turns red litmus blue
  • Universal indicator: red/orange/yellow = acid, green = neutral (pH 7), blue/purple = alkali
  • Acids release H⁺ ions in water. Alkalis release OH⁻ ions
  • An alkali is a base that dissolves in water
acid + metal → salt + hydrogen
acid + carbonate → salt + water + carbon dioxide
acid + alkali → salt + water  (neutralisation)
GasTestResult
Hydrogenlighted splint"pop" sound
Carbon dioxidebubble through limewaterwhite precipitate
Oxygenglowing splintrelights

Uses of neutralisation: antacids for indigestion, lime (calcium hydroxide) for acidic soil, toothpaste against mouth acid.

Examplehydrochloric acid + sodium hydroxide → sodium chloride + water
Watch out: copper and other unreactive metals do not react with dilute acids, so no hydrogen is given off.
